title: Ultrasonic Testing of Castings and Forgings | A388, A609
description: Ultrasonic testing of castings and forgings in the US to ASTM A388 and A609: straight-beam and angle-beam UT at foundries and forge shops. Request a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing of Castings and Forgings to ASTM A388 and A609 Across the United States
html:
Ultrasonic testing of castings and forgings uses a straight-beam probe, and angle-beam where the specification requires it, to find internal discontinuities such as shrinkage, porosity, inclusions, laps, bursts and cracks in heavy steel parts. Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to foundries, forge shops, machine shops and receiving docks across the United States and tests to the standard on your purchase order, typically ASTM A388 or A609. To scope it, request a UT inspection quote with the drawing and the specification.

What ultrasonic testing can find in castings and forgings

A casting solidifies from liquid, and the last metal to freeze can pull away from itself and leave shrinkage cavities, microshrinkage and gas porosity inside thick sections. Hot tears and cracks form at section changes. A forging is shaped by working solid metal, so its typical defects are different: internal bursts and cracks from heavy reduction, laps, seams, stringers and inclusions elongated by working, and in large ingots the center-line segregation and porosity that forging is supposed to consolidate. Ultrasonic testing sees through the full section, which is why purchasers specify it for thick shafts, rotors, rings, discs, pressure vessel forgings and heavy castings, where surface methods and a visual look say nothing about the interior.

Ultrasonic testing does not replace surface methods. A fine surface crack in a forging is better found with magnetic particle testing, and a casting surface porosity pattern shows well under penetrant. Many purchase orders call for both: ultrasonic testing for the volume, MT or PT for the surface. See the pages on magnetic particle testing and liquid penetrant testing.

The standards that set the examination

  • ASTM A388 / ASME SA-388: ultrasonic examination of heavy steel forgings, covering straight-beam scanning, angle-beam where specified, reference blocks and recording rules.
  • ASTM A609 / ASME SA-609: ultrasonic examination of carbon, low-alloy and martensitic stainless steel castings by longitudinal wave, with quality levels set by the order.
  • ASTM E114: straight-beam pulse-echo contact testing, used as a reference practice for method and equipment.
  • ASME Section V, Article 23: the ultrasonic standards (SA-388, SA-609, SE-114 and others) that ASME code sections incorporate by reference.
  • The purchase order or drawing: it names the standard, the reference reflector, the quality level and the acceptance limit. This is the document that decides what is rejectable.

The method overview is on the national ultrasonic testing page, and the written practice for the technique draws on the Article 23 and E114 practices.

Technique: probes, references and scanning

Castings and forgings are tested with a contact probe on a clean, machined or ground surface. Probe frequency is chosen for the material: lower frequencies penetrate coarse-grained cast steel, higher frequencies resolve small flaws in fine-grained wrought steel. A forging is typically scanned with a straight beam from the outside diameter and the faces, with the scan plan set by the shape: radial scans on shafts and bars, axial and radial scans on rings, and scans from several faces on blocks and discs. A388 also calls for angle-beam scanning of rings and hollow forgings where the specification requires it, to catch circumferentially oriented flaws that a radial beam cannot see.

The reference decides sensitivity. Under A388, sensitivity is set from the back reflection or from a flat-bottom-hole reference block of the sound path depth and diameter named by the order, and the technician uses a distance-amplitude correction or a documented procedure to evaluate indications at different depths. The technician watches for indications above the reference level, for loss of back reflection that points to a wide discontinuity or poor surface contact, and for linear or traveling indications that move as the probe moves, which suggest planar flaws. Castings add a complication: coarse grain scatters sound, causes grass-like noise on the screen and attenuates the back echo, so the acceptance rules in A609 work with the quality levels for the part, and the technician must tell grain noise from real flaws.

Surface, geometry and temperature

Surface condition is a specification item, not a courtesy. A388 and A609 expect a machined or ground surface at the scanning faces with the finish stated in the standard; an as-cast or scaly surface prevents coupling. Sound must also reach the volume you care about. Complex casting geometry, thin ribs, fillets and cored sections reflect sound from walls instead of from flaws, so the technician plans the scan to cover each accessible section and the report records what could not be tested. Parts are tested at ambient shop temperature, so hot-work temperature limits are not an issue, but a part pulled from heat treatment must be at ordinary temperature before the scan.

Where the testing happens

Castings and forgings are inspected at several points in the supply chain, and each point has its own planning.

Thickness, section size and sound path

Section thickness controls almost every setting in a casting or forging examination. The sound path to the far wall sets the back-reflection signal the technician watches, the depth of the flat-bottom-hole reference, and how many faces must be scanned to cover the volume. In thin sections near the scan face, the first part of the volume can sit inside the initial pulse dead zone, so the plan may call for a second scan from the opposite face or a dual-element probe to cover it. In heavy sections the sound path is long, attenuation grows, and the technician checks that the reference level still produces a usable signal at full depth before relying on the scan.

Wall thickness measurement is a separate job from flaw detection, even on the same part. A forged ring or shaft may need a thickness check to confirm machining stock or remaining section, and the report keeps those readings apart from the flaw indications so they are not confused. If you need both, say so in the quote request and each is written to its own procedure.

Cast and wrought material differences in practice

Different alloys behave differently under the probe. Carbon and low-alloy steel castings in the as-heat-treated condition test well with lower-frequency longitudinal waves. Martensitic stainless castings are covered by A609 but attenuate sound more. Austenitic stainless and nickel alloy castings have large columnar grain that makes meaningful ultrasonic examination very difficult, and those materials are usually outside what a contact method can reliably clear. Forgings in the quenched and tempered condition are usually fine-grained and test cleanly, while forgings that were not normalized can show noise from coarse structure. The technician records the grain noise level in the report so a reviewer can see how much margin there was.

What the report contains

  • Part number, heat or serial number, material, dimensions, heat treatment condition and the specification, edition and quality level
  • Procedure number and revision, probe type, frequency, scan plan and reference reflector
  • Equipment, calibration blocks and calibration checks, including the sensitivity setting and any distance-amplitude correction
  • Technician name and level, with the written practice the qualification sits under
  • Each recorded indication with location, depth, size or amplitude against the reference, and the accept or reject decision against the stated limit
  • Loss of back reflection and linear indication notes, areas not scanned, and a sketch or part map

A Level II technician performs and interprets the examination; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. For help writing a casting and forging procedure to your purchase specification, see NDT technical procedure development.

What to send for a quote

  • Purchase order, drawing or specification with the standard, edition, reference reflector and quality level
  • Material, heat treatment condition, dimensions and weight, and quantity of parts
  • Surface finish at the scan faces and whether parts will be machined before testing
  • Where the work will happen: foundry, forge shop, machine shop, receiving dock or customer plant
  • Whether MT or PT is also required, and any previous inspection records
  • Site address, handling support such as cranes and turning fixtures, and badging or safety requirements

Where we work in the United States

Casting and forging work follows the foundries, forge shops and heavy-industry plants. These city pages have local detail:

  • Birmingham: pipe, valve and steel castings across Alabama.
  • Detroit: automotive castings and forgings, press tooling and drivetrain parts.
  • Peoria: heavy equipment castings and forged components for construction and mining machinery.
  • Houston: valves, wellhead and subsea forgings and castings for energy equipment.
  • Chicago: steel, rail and heavy equipment castings and forgings.

Industry pages show how the same method looks by sector: steel mills, automotive, power generation, mining, oilfield equipment and rail.

Planning notes

Technicians are mobilized to the shop or dock for the agreed scope, and the work goes better when parts are laid out, numbered and accessible. Heavy parts need crane or fixture support from the site, because a 20-ton ring cannot be turned by one technician. The scan is slow on large parts, since every surface in the scan plan must be covered, so a realistic quote starts from the actual number and size of parts. Repair situations need the excavation sketch before the technician starts.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, which has its own licensing under 10 CFR Part 34 and Agreement State rules, so a purchase order that calls for radiography of castings has to be sent elsewhere. We do not offer specialist scanning techniques for complex geometry on this page, and we do not decide casting acceptance when the order assigns that to the buyer or its source inspector. Ultrasonic testing also does not replace chemistry, hardness or mechanical test requirements.

Training your own technicians

If your foundry or machine shop wants its own team, our UT Level 2 training covers straight-beam and angle-beam setup, reference blocks and indication evaluation, and the ultrasonic testing simulator offers practice with reflectors before technicians scan a real part. See also manufacturing NDT training. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its personnel, so the course supports your written practice.

faq.q: Which ultrasonic standard applies to steel castings?
faq.a: ASTM A609, or ASME SA-609 when an ASME code section calls for it, covers longitudinal-wave ultrasonic examination of carbon, low-alloy and martensitic stainless steel castings. The purchase order names the quality level and acceptance limit that applies to the specific part.

faq.q: Which standard applies to heavy steel forgings?
faq.a: ASTM A388, or ASME SA-388, covers ultrasonic examination of heavy steel forgings. It sets straight-beam scanning, references and recording rules, with angle-beam scanning of rings and hollow forgings where the order requires it.

faq.q: Why is ultrasonic testing of castings harder than forgings?
faq.a: Cast steel has coarse grain that scatters sound, raises background noise and weakens the back echo, so small flaws are harder to separate from grain noise. The standard and the quality level reflect this, and the technician sets the technique to the casting.

faq.q: What surface finish do I need before testing?
faq.a: The scanning faces should be machined or ground to the finish stated in the standard or on the order, with scale and as-cast roughness removed. A rough surface prevents coupling and loses sensitivity, so finish should be ready before our technician arrives.

faq.q: Can you test a part that is only rough machined?
faq.a: Yes, if the faces needed for the scan are accessible and meet the surface requirement. Testing at rough machine is common, because a finding at that stage costs less than one found after finish machining.

faq.q: Do you test forgings and castings that are already in service?
faq.a: Yes, parts removed for refurbishment, such as shafts, rolls and rings, can be examined with straight-beam and angle-beam techniques where the geometry allows. The report notes areas that could not be reached and anything affected by service condition.

faq.q: Do you do radiography of castings?
faq.a: No. Industrial radiography in the United States is licensed under 10 CFR Part 34 and Agreement State rules, and Atlantis does not perform it. If the order requires radiography, we say so at the quote stage.

faq.q: Who decides whether a casting or forging is accepted?
faq.a: The purchase order, drawing or code decides. Our report states the indications against the stated criteria, and the buyer, the owner or its source inspector makes the final decision where the order gives it to them.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote?
faq.a: Send the purchase order or specification, drawing, material and heat treatment, part sizes and quantity, surface finish, location of the work and any MT or PT requirements. Weight and handling arrangements are also needed for large parts.
